metric_rationale: This design makes the highest-validity cue (feature 0) discriminate in the opposite direction to the majority of the remaining cues on every trial. Take The Best therefore predicts the option favored by the first discriminating cue, while Tallying predicts the opposite option favored by the lower-cue tally. The metric is the proportion of trials on which a subject follows the first discriminating cue. It uses all 96 trials per subject, keeping per-subject binomial variance small (about p(1-p)/96). Under TTB the score is above 0.5, approaching 1 with stronger beta; under Tallying it is below 0.5 because the top cue is the minority tally cue. The design balances top-cue-favors-A and top-cue-favors-B trials, so the raw proportion is not confounded by position bias. This gives a reliable mean separation with tight between-subject variance at N=25.

The metric contrasts, trial by trial, whether a choice follows the full-tally prediction or the stopping-at-the-first-discriminating-cue prediction. Because feature 0 is tied everywhere, feature 1 is the first discriminating cue for Take The Best. On every non-tied trial in this design, the second cue prediction and the tally prediction point in opposite directions, so tally_score - second_score is positive when choices use lower cues and negative when choices stop at feature 1. Averaging over all 96 trials per subject makes the statistic stable under response noise while preserving the large direction-of-effect gap between Tallying and Take The Best.

This is the observed within-tally-difference split by the first discriminating TTB cue. Feature 0 is tied on every trial, so TTB drops to feature 1 (validity 0.80), which always discriminates. I classify every trial by whether feature 1 favors A or B, and subtract the proportion of A choices in the feature-1-favors-B class from the proportion in the feature-1-favors-A class. The trial set has equal feature-1 direction counts within each tally difference d = A_wins - B_wins, so pure Tallying predicts the same A-choice probability in the two classes and the metric has expectation 0. The advocated TTB/Tallying mixture instead shifts the favored class by q times the near-deterministic TTB preference gap; with q near 0.25 and beta_ttb near 5.25 the expected metric is approximately 0.247. Each subject contributes 48 trials per class, keeping between-subject noise low.

All 32 unique pairs in this design have equal feature-win tallies for A and B, so pure Tallying predicts an A-choice probability of 0.5 on every trial. The TTB mixture violates this only when the first validity-ordered discriminating feature favors one option. The metric classifies each trial by that first discriminator using the validity order 0.92, 0.88, 0.80, 0.72, 0.65, 0.60, 0.55, 0.52, then returns the difference in A-choice rate between first-discriminator-favors-A and first-discriminator-favors-B trials. Pure Tallying gives approximately 0.0, while the mixture gives approximately 0.62 minus 0.38, about 0.25, providing a large and stable contrast.

The metric measures the signed effect of the highest-validity cue: mean P(choose A) on trials where feature 0 favors A minus mean P(choose A) on trials where feature 0 favors B. All pairs in this design are feature-win tally neutral and feature 0 always discriminates, so tallying contributes 0.5 in both directions. The advocated forward TTB mixture therefore predicts a positive value near 0.25, while the competing backward-heavy mixture predicts a negative value near -0.35. Each subject has 48 trials in each top-cue direction, so this contrast has a large between-theory gap and only modest per-subject binomial variability.

This contrast uses the top-vs-bottom conflict trials where the first validity cue and the full tally point in the same direction. In the competing model, the TTB route and tallying both select the top-cued option on these trials, so choice of A is near 1 for top-A trials and near 0 for top-B trials, giving a pooled difference near +1. In the advocated model, the backward lexicographic route partially cancels the top cue: top-A trials stay near 0.47 and top-B trials stay near 0.53, so the same difference is near -0.06. The metric uses 36 top-A and 36 top-B trials per subject, making per-subject estimates reasonably tight.

This metric recodes every trial relative to the option favored by the highest-validity cue (feature 0) and measures the proportion of top-cue choices on conflict-gate trials, defined as rows where the top-cue option does not trail the opposite option in the feature-win tally (top_wins - other_wins >= 0). The advocated conflict-gated model suspends tallying in these rows and boosts a strong backward/low-cue route, predicting a low and flat top-cue choice rate around 0.17. The competing stable mixture keeps all three routes active, so its top-cue choice rate increases with the tally and averages around 0.43 on the same rows. Because each subject contributes many such rows, the per-subject estimate is stable while the model separation is large.

Score every trial as 1 if the response selected the option favored by the lowest-validity cue (feature 7), otherwise 0. The metric is the mean score on conflict-gate-active trials minus the mean score on the remaining inactive trials. The advocated stable mixture predicts identical choice probabilities for matched active and inactive trials because the forward winner, backward winner, and tally difference are matched, so this contrast is expected to be near zero with only binomial noise. The competing conflict-gated model predicts a large positive contrast because active conflict trials suspend tallying and strongly use a backward scan that stops at feature 7. With 48 active and 48 inactive trials per subject, the within-subject variability is small.

This metric estimates the signed trial-type effect created by the tied low-validity cue manipulation. For each subject and each top-cue direction, it classifies trials by whether the advocated conflict gate is live using the highest-validity cue, the tied lowest-validity cues, and the tally direction. It then computes signed choose-A proportions, oriented by top-cue direction, and takes inactive minus active within each top direction before averaging across the two top directions. The advocated conflict-gated model predicts a large positive value because the gate reverses the choice away from the top cue when active, while the stable-mixture model predicts approximately zero because its forward scan stops before the tied low cue and its backward scan stops at the first tied low cue, making the two trial types indistinguishable.

This metric isolates the predicted conflict-gate effect. Feature 0 is the unique highest-validity cue, so every response is recoded as choose-top: 1 if the subject chose the option favored by feature 0, otherwise 0. Gate-active trials are those where feature 7 is tied; in this design that is exactly when the lowest-validity cue set is uniform and the competing theory's conflict gate switches on, producing a strong backward-lexicographic shift away from the top cue. Gate-inactive trials are those where feature 7 discriminates in the same direction as feature 0, so the competing theory remains in its baseline mixture. The metric is the choose-top rate on gate-inactive trials minus the choose-top rate on gate-active trials. Under the advocated stable-mixture theory, forward lexicographic scanning stops at feature 0, backward lexicographic scanning stops at feature 6, and tally differences are balanced across the gate manipulation, so feature 7 is irrelevant and the expected metric is zero. Under the competing conflict-gated theory, tied feature 7 sharply lowers choose-top responding on gate-active trials, so the metric is expected to be large and positive. The contrast is within-subject and uses roughly 48 trials per condition, keeping per-subject variance manageable.
